questions.q: Per this lesson's worked example, why does the Claim-approval automation end up using both Flow and Apex rather than entirely one or the other?
options: Because Salesforce requires every automation to include at least one line of Apex
Because Flow cannot update any field on a related record under any circumstances

Because applying Lesson 5's factors piece by piece shows most of the requirement (status updates, threshold check, task creation) fits declarative tools well, while only the complex notification-formatting piece meets the bar for Apex
Because Apex is always required whenever an email needs to be sent
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that a realistic requirement usually splits: most of the Claim-approval logic is comfortably declarative, with only the genuinely complex notification-formatting piece justifying a small, focused Apex method.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between before-save and after-save automation, as this lesson describes it?
options: Before-save automation runs before the record is committed and can modify field values without a separate save operation; after-save automation runs once the record is already committed, for actions depending on the saved record
There is no real difference -- both run at the exact same point in a transaction
Before-save automation only applies to Apex triggers, never to Flow
After-save automation always runs faster than before-save automation
questions.explain: Before-save logic can modify the record's own fields efficiently as part of the same save; after-save logic runs once the record is already committed, which is needed for actions like sending a notification about the saved state.

questions.q: Why does this lesson connect Flow sprawl (Lesson 9) and the one-trigger-per-object pattern (Lesson 6) to order-of-execution risk specifically?
options: Those patterns have no connection to order-of-execution risk at all
Order-of-execution risk only exists when Apex is used, never with multiple Flows
One-trigger-per-object eliminates governor limits entirely
Having fewer, well-organized pieces of automation on an object reduces the number of order-of-execution conflicts an architect has to reason about, not just the maintenance burden
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties these earlier patterns to reducing order-of-execution conflicts: fewer, consolidated pieces of automation on the same object are easier to reason about in terms of relative execution order.

questions.q: What does the lesson's example automation-approach design note include, that makes it a defensible design decision rather than an unexplained one?
options: Just a list of object names with no further explanation
The specific automation structure (which Flow, which trigger condition) plus the rationale for which piece used Apex and why, tied back to Lesson 5's factors
Only the names of the developers who will build it
A complete Apex class with no explanation of the reasoning behind it
questions.explain: The worked design note states the structure and explicitly ties the Apex piece's justification back to Lesson 5's factors (the notification-formatting complexity), which is what makes the decision defensible rather than arbitrary.

questions.q: In the Lab's variation where the notification email becomes simple, fixed-text, and templated with no attachments, what does this lesson imply about whether the Apex piece still earns its place?
options: Apex is always required for any email notification, regardless of complexity
The automation must stay exactly as designed regardless of changed requirements

Once the complexity that originally justified Apex (formatting, attachments assembled from multiple records) is removed, the factors from Lesson 5 would need to be re-evaluated, and a simple templated email likely no longer meets the bar for programmatic logic
Flow can never send any kind of email notification
questions.explain: The lesson's framework requires re-applying the actual factors to the actual requirement -- if the complexity that justified Apex is gone, the declarative option should be re-considered rather than keeping Apex out of habit.
